blindSummary:
The legal framework here is mid-transition. Public incitement to hatred based on gender identity is a criminal offence (2015), and gender identity is an aggravating factor in hate crime (2017). A legal gender recognition bill (on a self-determination basis) was approved by the cabinet in September 2022 and is pending in parliament; until it passes, legal gender recognition requires surgery under a 2002 registry law — a resident-facing gap.

No traveller-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues (the country is a member of a regional union), and tourist infrastructure is developed and accustomed to diverse visitors. Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the non-discrimination framework, and the country's division matters: the part outside government control (held de facto by a neighbouring state's administration) runs its own legal regime — there, legal gender recognition requires surgical proof, protections are weaker and enforcement less documented — so travellers should treat that part as closer to the neighbouring state's risk profile.
blindOutOfScope: The country's division and the pending legal-recognition bill are noted above; legal-gender-recognition requirements are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: UN periodic-review advocacy sheet for this country's 4th cycle (2024) on the situation of LGBTI persons: assesses implementation of the cycle-3 recommendations. Notes progress: a 2015 law criminalises public incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity; a 2017 amendment adds prejudice motivation as an aggravating factor. Outstanding: gender identity not yet a prohibited discrimination ground in equal-treatment legislation, no action plan against homophobia/transphobia, and pending legislation on transgender persons.

A regional body's network of legal experts, country report on gender equality in this country (2024, reporting period 2023): how the regional union's equality rules are transposed into national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

The main national LGBTI organisation's presentation for this country's UN periodic review: lists prior recommendations (anti-discrimination, hate-speech criminalisation, victim support, enactment of transgender-persons legislation) and developments, including the 2015 criminal-code amendment covering SOGI incitement.

The national LGBTI organisation's booklet on legal gender recognition (part of a regionally funded diversity project): describes the association's solidarity line (7 days/week, confidential psychosocial, legal and social support for LGBTI+ people on identity, education, work, family, shelter, health, military service), psychologist and legal-expert networks, and legal-gender-recognition issues - covering both the government-controlled areas and the part outside government control.

International LGBTI organisation's report on SOGIESC recommendations at the 32nd session of the UN review working group (Jan-Feb 2019): includes this country's chapter - summarises SOGIESC remarks, advanced questions and recommendations for this country among 14 states reviewed.

The regional expert network's country report on non-discrimination in this country (2020, reporting period 2019): transposition and implementation of the regional union's equality directives, including SOGI grounds in national law.

LGBTQ+ news outlet (Oct 2013): this country amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity (up to 3 years' imprisonment or a fine of 5,000 units of national currency); workplace protections for LGBT people added in 2004.
blindLocalsOnly: The pending self-determination legal-gender-recognition bill and the current surgery requirement under the 2002 registry law are resident-facing.
